title: Act on a chosen responsibility while a meaning question stays open

sections.title: Understand the distinction
sections.body: A local responsibility can have a reason even while an ultimate meaning question remains unanswered. Repetition does not by itself make a task futile; its beneficiary and actual use matter.

sections.title: Complete fictional practice material
sections.body: Complete case: a shared desk’s pencil belongs in its cup, the ruler in the flat tray and blank paper on shelf A. Jo may return these three items; no other belongings may move. A reader is expected later but has given no feedback. Ten minutes are available. Jo feels the routine is repetitive and does not expect inspiration.

sections.title: Work through the supplied case
sections.body: Return or map the three items to their authorized places, state the local purpose and identify what would show useful conduct rather than only intention.

sections.title: Try a different case before checking
sections.body: A recurrent task serves nobody under the current arrangement and repeatedly displaces essential rest. Must its repetition still be defended as meaningful?

checks.title: Compare reasoning and review the supplied result
checks.body: The mapping makes those items available as agreed. Later fiction: all three are returned in 4 minutes; the next reader finds the ruler but says nothing about the others. Jo’s mood is unchanged. Specific usefulness is supported for the ruler, not a universal meaning result. Partial: list the task without doing or simulating it. Incorrect: infer unchanged mood means no useful action occurred.
criteria: The local beneficiary and purpose are concrete
Actual conduct and observed use are separate
Mood does not determine whether a duty was served

checks.title: Check the changed case
checks.body: No. Reassess actual need, authority to stop and who might rely on it. Chosen responsibility is not a command to preserve every repetitive demand.
